conceptPrimer.heading: Band Gaps and the Negative Temperature Coefficient
conceptPrimer.proseLatex: Room-temperature band gaps: $E_g \approx 0.72\ \text{eV}$ (Ge) and $1.12\ \text{eV}$ (Si). Heat shakes more electrons across the gap, so resistance FALLS as temperature rises — semiconductors carry a NEGATIVE temperature coefficient of resistance (metals the opposite). Micro-check: Ge conducts measurably better than Si at the same doping precisely because its smaller gap frees more carriers.

conceptPrimer.heading: Doping: Donors, Acceptors and Neutrality
conceptPrimer.proseLatex: Pentavalent Group-15 donors (P, As, Sb) create $n$-type (electron majority; fixed positive donor ions); trivalent Group-13 acceptors (B, Al, Ga, In) create $p$-type. Both crystals remain ELECTRICALLY NEUTRAL — '$n$-type' names the majority MOBILE carrier, never a net charge. Micro-check: a phosphorus atom donates one electron and stays as an immobile $\text{P}^+$ ion — the charges cancel.

conceptPrimer.heading: Mass-Action Law and Conductivity
conceptPrimer.proseLatex: At equilibrium, $n \cdot p = n_i^2$ holds in intrinsic AND doped material: heavy doping of one carrier starves the other. Drift conductivity $\sigma = q(n\mu_n + p\mu_p)$, and the thermal voltage $V_T = \frac{kT}{q} \approx 26\ \text{mV}$ at 300 K recurs in every diode/transistor equation. Micro-check: Si ($n_i = 1.5\times10^{10}\ \text{cm}^{-3}$) doped $N_D = 2.25\times10^{15}$: $p_0 = \frac{2.25\times10^{20}}{2.25\times10^{15}} = 10^5\ \text{cm}^{-3}$ — ten orders below the majority.

conceptPrimer.heading: The p-n Junction and Its Bias Behaviour
conceptPrimer.proseLatex: Cut-in voltage $\approx 0.7\ \text{V}$ (Si), $0.3\ \text{V}$ (Ge), falling $\sim 2\ \text{mV}/^\circ\text{C}$. Forward bias NARROWS the depletion layer (current flows exponentially); reverse bias WIDENS it — the voltage-dependent junction capacitance $C_j$ is the varactor's tuning mechanism. Micro-check: double forward voltage and the forward current multiplies ~tenfold per $60\ \text{mV}$ — the diode law's steepness.

conceptPrimer.heading: Zener Regulation and the Rectifier Benchmarks
conceptPrimer.proseLatex: A heavily doped Zener works in REVERSE BREAKDOWN as a shunt regulator: clamped voltage, absorbing current swings. Rectifier roster: Half-Wave — $\eta_{\max} = 40.6\%$, ripple factor $1.21$, ripple frequency $f$; Centre-Tap Full-Wave — $81.2\%$, RF $0.482$, $2f$, but PIV $= 2V_m$ per diode; Bridge Full-Wave — $81.2\%$, $2f$, and the gentler PIV $= V_m$. Micro-check: at $V_m = 50\ \text{V}$, CT diodes must survive $100\ \text{V}$ reverse; bridge diodes only $50\ \text{V}$.

conceptPrimer.heading: BJT, MOSFET and CMOS Logic
conceptPrimer.proseLatex: A BJT is a bipolar CURRENT-controlled device: $I_E = I_B + I_C$. In the ACTIVE region (E-B forward, C-B reverse) it amplifies with $\beta = \frac{I_C}{I_B} = \frac{\alpha}{1-\alpha}$; cutoff (both reverse) and saturation (both forward) are the switch states. A MOSFET is unipolar, VOLTAGE-controlled with near-infinite gate impedance; CMOS pairs a PMOS pull-up with NMOS pull-down for near-zero static power and rail-to-rail noise margins. Micro-check: $\alpha = 0.98$: $\beta = 49$ and $I_E = (1+\beta)I_B = 50\,I_B$ — the base current is the tiny remainder.

mcqSelfTest.explanation: Mobile electrons are balanced by fixed positive donor ions — neutrality holds for every doping.

mcqSelfTest.stemLatex: For a bridge rectifier vs a centre-tapped full-wave rectifier, the diode PIV respectively is:
mcqSelfTest.explanation: Bridge diodes see only $V_m$; centre-tap diodes see $2V_m$ — the bridge's quiet advantage.

mcqSelfTest.stemLatex: The ripple frequency of a full-wave rectifier fed at 50 Hz is:
mcqSelfTest.explanation: Both half-cycles conduct: $f_{\text{ripple}} = 2f = 100\ \text{Hz}$ (a half-wave rectifier stays at 50 Hz).

mcqSelfTest.stemLatex: The maximum theoretical rectification efficiency of a half-wave rectifier is:
mcqSelfTest.explanation: HWR tops out at $40.6\%$; full-wave doubles it to $81.2\%$.

mcqSelfTest.stemLatex: A Zener diode used as a voltage regulator operates in:
mcqSelfTest.explanation: Heavily doped, it clamps at its breakdown voltage while shunting load — regulation lives in reverse breakdown.

mcqSelfTest.stemLatex: The cut-in voltage of a silicon diode at room temperature is approximately:
mcqSelfTest.explanation: $\approx 0.7\ \text{V}$ for Si ($0.3\ \text{V}$ Ge), falling about $2\ \text{mV}/^\circ\text{C}$ with heat.

mcqSelfTest.stemLatex: A MOSFET differs from a BJT chiefly because it is:
mcqSelfTest.explanation: MOSFETs are unipolar, voltage-controlled; $I_G \approx 0$ — no steady gate current.

mcqSelfTest.stemLatex: The main reason CMOS logic dissipates almost no static power is:

options.latex: one network conducts per input state, never both

mcqSelfTest.explanation: The PMOS pull-up and NMOS pull-down never conduct simultaneously in a static state — the supply sees no direct path.

memoryHooks: Ge 0.72, Si 1.12 — smaller gap, earlier conduction.
Heat frees carriers: semiconductors fall in resistance.
Donors give electrons (n), acceptors give holes (p) — crystal stays neutral.
$np = n_i^2$: feed one carrier, starve the other.
CT pays double PIV ($2V_m$); the bridge pays $V_m$.
Zener regulates by breaking down in reverse.
CMOS: never both networks on — static power ~0.
commonMistakes: Calling an n-type crystal negatively charged.
Using $n_i$ instead of $n_i^2$ in the mass-action division.
Assigning PIV $= 2V_m$ to bridge rectifiers (that's centre-tap).
Expecting a Zener to regulate in forward bias.
Forgetting the $-2\ \text{mV}/^\circ\text{C}$ drift of cut-in voltage.
Claiming MOSFETs need steady gate current.
examChecklist: Recite $E_g$ for Ge/Si and the negative temperature coefficient.
State neutrality of doped crystals before carrier talk.
Apply $np = n_i^2$ for minority concentration; keep exponents straight.
Quote cut-in voltages and their temperature drift.
Map every rectifier to $\eta$, RF, ripple frequency and PIV.
Name the three BJT regions with junction biases.
Contrast BJT (current, bipolar) with MOSFET (voltage, unipolar).
Justify CMOS low static power by the complementary pair.
Use $V_T \approx 26\ \text{mV}$ wherever the diode law appears.
